# Event and log data {#sec-events}

::: {.content-hidden}
PLAN (replaces the earlier "Network intrusions and fraud" chapter, Oct 2026)

Organise by data type, like the other chapters, with cyber-security and fraud as
the motivating examples. Generic methods applied to intrusion/fraud data would
just repeat Chapters 6, 7 and 9, so focus on what is genuinely new:

1. Event data as a data type: irregularly timestamped, marked event streams
   (logins, connections, transactions), often with high-cardinality categorical
   marks (user, host, port, merchant). Not covered by Chapter 10 (regular series),
   Chapter 12 (graphs) or Chapter 14 (categorical). Point processes, inter-arrival
   surprisals, burst detection.

2. Entity-level baselines: "unusual for this user" rather than "unusual overall".
   Peer group analysis (Bolton & Hand, 2001; review in Statistical Science, 2002).

3. Combining weak evidence: attacks are often chains of individually normal events
   (e.g., lateral movement). Combining p-values across events and entities; FDR
   control over many entities; mid-p-values for discrete data (Heard,
   Rubin-Delanchy, Turcotte, Adams), linking to surprisal probabilities with ties.

4. Brief discussion only: delayed and biased labels (chargebacks; only flagged
   cases get investigated), concept drift, and flawed benchmarks (McHugh, 2000, on
   DARPA/KDD-99; Sommer & Paxson, 2010, "Outside the closed world").

Candidate data: LANL authentication data (Kent, 2015), subsampled (~1 billion
events in full).

Material to place elsewhere:
- Adversarial anomalies (attackers deliberately mimic typical behaviour, so low
  surprisal does not imply benign; Wagner & Soto, 2002): paragraph in
  @sec-spurious.
- Base rates and alert budgets (Axelsson, 2000): ranking/precision-at-k framing in
  Chapter 4 or the Chapter 7 summary.
:::
